items.tx:
Imagine being a federal judge looking at a Senate race where, according to the New York Times, people tied to Mary Peltola's campaign and the DSCC went digging through voter rolls to find a retired teacher from Petersburg named Daniel J. Sullivan, and he ends up on the same ballot as Senator Dan Sullivan in a ranked choice state that was already built to confuse people… and your answer is that nobody can do anything about it.

That is what Judge Sharon Gleason just did. She threw out the DOJ lawsuit to set aside the ballots cast for the decoy Dan so the fraud could actually be investigated, and she did it for three reasons that should make every voter in this country sick. The federal government lacks standing. Separating those ballots would violate ballot secrecy. And it is too late to change anything this close to Election Day.

There is a federal criminal probe with grand jury subpoenas out, the Governor of Alaska ordered his own state investigation, and the court's answer is basically tough luck, the clock ran out, count them anyway. Too late? Too late for who? The people who planned this knew exactly when to run it, and they knew a court would say the words "too close to the election" because that is what courts say every single time the deck is stacked and the timing is the whole trick.

And ballot secrecy… really? Nobody is asking to see who you voted for. They are asking to hold the votes cast for a candidate who may only be on that ballot because somebody went shopping for a man with the right name. How is protecting that a defense of democracy? How do you look the people of Alaska in the eye and tell them the system cannot pause for a scheme everyone can see?

Peltola says she knew nothing. Maybe. But you have seen this movie before, the operatives do the dirty work, the candidate keeps clean hands, the judge says no standing, and the result gets certified long before anyone gets to the truth. Same same.

This is institutional rot dressed up in a robe, and the only thing a federal court managed to protect today was the scheme itself.

Judge Gleason, you were handed a chance to protect the integrity of a United States Senate election and you hid behind a calendar.

DOJ, appeal it today and do not stop until every person who recruited that decoy is sitting under oath.

Pray, Stand, Speak, ACT.

Ms. Ronya Othmann,
You are neither in a position nor qualified to dictate terms to the Iranian people, nor do you have the authority to determine who genuinely represents them.
Prince Reza Pahlavi is a political representative of the Iranian people and a figure whom a significant portion of Iranians recognize as their representative and political leader. It is the Iranian people who will decide their country's political future—not you, not the political movements you support, and certainly not Kurdish political leaders in Iraq and Syria. None of these individuals or movements represents the Iranian people or has the right to speak on their behalf.
If you genuinely care about human rights, civil liberties, and women's rights, you should demonstrate the same concern for the issues and crises within the communities where your own political sphere of influence lies. These include women's rights, reports of female genital mutilation in certain areas, press freedom, the treatment of journalists, and the situation of political prisoners in the Kurdistan Region of Iraq.
Human rights cannot be defended selectively. You cannot presume to dictate political solutions for Iran while remaining silent about, or overlooking, human rights violations and serious problems within your own political sphere.
My message to you is straightforward: stay out of Iran's internal affairs, respect the political choices of the Iranian people, and before attempting to dictate terms to others, take a serious look at the problems and political responsibilities within your own sphere.
The Iranian people do not need guardians or imposed spokespersons. They know whom they recognize as their representative, and they will not allow others to make decisions on their behalf.
As the great Persian poet Saadi Shirazi wrote:
"Speak less, but choose your words like pearls, For words, once spoken, can fill the world."
